evidence.claim: A highway brought to the lakeshore, linking beaches and small communities
evidence.quote: This byway extends from St. Ignace to Manistique, and offers drivers scenic vistas, beautiful white-sand beaches, and highlights the small communities found between the cities of St. Ignace and Manistique.

evidence.claim: A highway brought to the lakeshore
evidence.quote: others pushed an originally inland routing of US 2 closer to the Lake Michigan shoreline.

evidence.claim: US 2 follows Lake Michigan through Naubinway, crosses the Cut River high above its valley, and passes through Hiawatha National Forest near Brevort.
evidence.quote: runs to the south of Engadine to follow the Lake Michigan shoreline through Naubinway. After passing the community of Epoufette, US 2 crosses the Cut River Bridge, 147 feet (45 m) over the Cut River. The highway crosses into the eastern unit of the Hiawatha National Forest near Brevort

evidence.claim: The Top of the Lake route belongs to the Pure Michigan Byways program.
evidence.quote: was designated the Top of the Lake Scenic Byway in the Pure Michigan Byways program on October 9, 2017.

evidence.claim: The Eastern Upper Peninsula Regional Planning and Development Commission highlights its white-sand beaches, views and small communities between St. Ignace and Manistique.
evidence.quote: This byway extends from St. Ignace to Manistique, and offers drivers scenic vistas, beautiful white-sand beaches, and highlights the small communities found between the cities of St. Ignace and Manistique.

evidence.claim: The highway did not always keep so close to the water.
evidence.quote: others pushed an originally inland routing of US 2 closer to the Lake Michigan shoreline.

evidence.claim: In 1936, the Michigan State Highway Department began a new lakeshore road into St. Ignace, replacing an inland routing from Brevort through Moran.
evidence.quote: The MSHD started construction in 1936 on a new road that rerouted US 2 into St. Ignace for the first time. Between Brevort and Moran, US 2 previously followed Worth Road inland to the Tahquamenon Trail to meet the northern extension of US 31 into the Upper Peninsula. The new routing took US 2 along the lakeshore into St. Ignace.

evidence.claim: In 1941, another realignment carried US 2 from Gould City through Naubinway and along the lake to Epoufette.
evidence.quote: Additional realignments were completed by the MSHD to move US 2 to its modern lakeshore routing between Gould City and Epoufette in 1941. The new highway traveled due east from Gould City to Naubinway and then along the lake to Epoufette.

evidence.claim: Driving west from St. Ignace, follow the shore toward Brevort, where Lake Michigan and Brevoort Lake flank the road.
evidence.quote: The highway crosses into the eastern unit of the Hiawatha National Forest near Brevort, running between Lake Michigan and Brevoort Lake in the process. The road continues along the Lake Michigan shoreline

evidence.claim: Cross the Cut River before Epoufette and continue through Naubinway; US 2 then passes south of Engadine and heads inland past Gould City to Blaney Park.
evidence.quote: From Blaney Park, US 2 turns due east and crosses into Mackinac County west of Gould City. Where it intersects a former routing, the main highway crosses the CN Railway one last time and runs to the south of Engadine to follow the Lake Michigan shoreline through Naubinway. After passing the community of Epoufette, US 2 crosses the Cut River Bridge

evidence.claim: Beyond Gulliver, the road returns to Lake Michigan at Manistique and crosses the river that gives the city its name.
evidence.quote: The roadway runs along Lake Michigan to Manistique, crossing the Manistique River. The trunkline turns inland approaching Gulliver and then turns north-northeast to Blaney Park.

evidence.claim: the river that gives the city its name
evidence.quote: The city is named after the river.

evidence.claim: Cut River Bridge carries US 2 across a valley 147 feet below the roadway.
evidence.quote: The bridge carries traffic on US 2 above and spans the Cut River Valley, 147 feet (45 m) below.

evidence.claim: The State Highway Department designed the crossing, and W.J. Meagher and Sons began construction in 1941.
evidence.quote: The State Highway Department designed this structure, and W.J. Meagher and Sons, Contractors, built it. Actual construction began in 1941.

evidence.claim: Wartime demand for steel halted work until after World War II.
evidence.quote: Due to the demand for steel during World War II, construction on the bridge was halted until after the war.

evidence.claim: The finished cantilever spans 641 feet and contains 888 short tons of structural steel.
evidence.quote: it is 641 feet (195 m) long and contains 888 short tons (793 long tons; 806 t)  of structural steel.

evidence.claim: A wooden staircase was added later to reach the valley.
evidence.quote: There is a long wooden staircase to the valley below that was constructed some time after the construction of the bridge itself.

evidence.claim: Under the east end, an office door bears a brass plaque inscribed “T. Troll.”
evidence.quote: On the east end of the bridge, there is an office door built under the main structure with a brass plaque inscribed "T. Troll".

evidence.claim: The sidewalk guardrails are original; the steel members have extensive latticing.
evidence.quote: The structure has extensive latticing on its members, which are all very massive. The bridge retains original standard-plan metal guardrails on the sidewalks that flank the roadway on each side.

evidence.claim: Lake Michigan supplied Naubinway with both a harbor and a place on a territorial boundary.
evidence.quote: Naubinway also benefited from being a port community on Lake Michigan.

evidence.claim: The lake’s northernmost point helped define the western boundary of Michigan Territory in 1805; the territory expanded westward in 1818.
evidence.quote: This point was used to draw the westernmost boundary of the Michigan Territory when it was created in 1805.  West of this point belonged to the Indiana Territory until the Michigan Territory expanded westward in 1818.

evidence.claim: By 1880, Naubinway was a lumbering community, with commercial fishing growing alongside the timber trade.
evidence.quote: Naubinway began as a lumbering community at the beginning of the lumber boom in the Upper Peninsula by 1880.

evidence.claim: Fishing continued after lumber declined at the turn of the century.
evidence.quote: In addition to the growing lumber industry, the community also had a large commercial fishing industry. When the lumber industry declined after the turn of the century, the fishing industry continued.

evidence.claim: Millecoquins Point forms the natural harbor, which contains a park and marina.
evidence.quote: This cape creates a small natural harbor known as Naubinway Harbor, which contains a park and marina called the Naubinway–Garfield Township Marina.

evidence.claim: with commercial fishing growing alongside the timber trade
evidence.quote: In addition to the growing lumber industry, the community also had a large commercial fishing industry.

evidence.claim: Manistique takes its name from its river, but not its original spelling.
evidence.quote: With the river originally spelled Monistique, a spelling error in the city charter led to its current spelling.

evidence.claim: The river was spelled Monistique; a mistake in the city charter produced the name used now.
evidence.quote: With the river originally spelled Monistique, a spelling error in the city charter led to its current spelling.

evidence.claim: At the river mouth, a natural harbor has been improved with dredging, breakwaters and the Manistique East Breakwater Light.
evidence.quote: The city lies on the north shore of Lake Michigan at the mouth of the Manistique River, which forms a natural harbor that has been improved with breakwaters, dredging, and the Manistique East Breakwater Light.

evidence.claim: Timber and pig iron shipped daily from this harbor at the beginning of the twentieth century.
evidence.quote: At the beginning of the 20th century, Manistique was a boom town, with timber and pig iron shipping from the harbor daily.

evidence.claim: The east light first shone on August 17, 1916, after completion of the east breakwater the previous year.
evidence.quote: The east breakwater itself was not completed until 1915, at which time work began on the east breakwater light and a station keeper's house at the foot of the breakwater.  Construction was completed in August, and the new light was lit on August 17, 1916.

evidence.claim: The new highway initially detoured around Cut River, where steel shortages during World War II delayed the bridge. Completion came after the war.
evidence.quote: The new highway was detoured around the Cut River Bridge until it was completed in 1946 after construction delays over steel shortages during World War II.

evidence.claim: Original metal guardrails remain on the sidewalks on both sides of the roadway.
evidence.quote: The bridge retains original standard-plan metal guardrails on the sidewalks that flank the roadway on each side.

evidence.claim: US 2 was rerouted through the community along Lake Michigan beginning in the 1940s, providing a major transportation route.
evidence.quote: Beginning in the 1940s, U.S. Route 2 was constructed and rerouted to pass directly through the community of Naubinway along Lake Michigan. U.S. Route 2 provided a major transportation route through the area.

evidence.claim: Its square tower is assembled from prefabricated steel plates bolted together.
evidence.quote: The tower is made of prefabricated steel plates bolted together and lagged to the foundation.

flags: Cache 01 contains only a Wayback wrapper, not the MDOT driving guide. Dropped unsupported tall bluffs, dipping road, empty beaches and 92-mile length; no cached driving time.
Cache 30 dates Cut River Bridge completion to 1946; cache 31 says built in 1947. Used only the supported postwar sequence.

Corridor endpoints differ: regional commission says St. Ignace–Manistique; cache 30 describes the 2017 designation as Thompson–St. Ignace. Followed the commission and assigned story extent without asserting an exact designation boundary.
Moments run westward, in descending strip-map miles, matching the overview. Current moments have no motifs field; absence preserved.
